properties.title: AWS us-east-1 control plane concentration
properties.one_line: IAM, Route 53, and CloudFront control planes all run in one county in Virginia — every AWS customer worldwide is downstream of us-east-1 whether they deploy there or not.
properties.dependency: AWS Identity & Access Management (IAM), Route 53 DNS management, CloudFront provisioning, AWS Organizations, and DynamoDB Global Tables all have control planes that require us-east-1. Customers deploying in eu-west-1 or ap-southeast-1 still depend on us-east-1 for authentication, DNS changes, and account management.
properties.consequence: When us-east-1 fails, services in other regions can't authenticate, can't update DNS, can't provision new resources. The December 2021 outage proved this: services not explicitly using us-east-1 failed because their control plane dependencies lived there.
properties.who_controls: Amazon Web Services. $35B invested in Northern Virginia alone. 65 data centers in Loudoun County. $576M in annual local tax revenue (30%+ of county budget). Same county driving PJM capacity cost explosion.

properties.title: AWS December 2021 outage cascade — three failures in three weeks
properties.affected_scope: Disney+, Netflix, Slack, Robinhood, Coinbase, Ticketmaster, Venmo, Instacart, Roku, Kindle, IRS, NY Court System
properties.one_line: Three major AWS outages in three weeks (Dec 7, 15, 22). The first took down Netflix and Disney+ for 7 hours. The blast radius proved that most of the internet is one region failure away from dark.
properties.dependency: Dec 7: us-east-1 network device overload cascaded to EC2, S3, DynamoDB, ELB (7+ hours). Dec 15: us-west-2 impacted Slack, DoorDash, PlayStation, Zoom (1+ hour). Dec 22: us-east-1 power failure took down Slack, Okta, NY Court System.
properties.consequence: Billions in estimated economic losses. Ring doorbells stopped working. Robinhood trading halted. IRS website went down. NY state court filing system offline. Each outage revealed new dependency chains nobody had mapped.
properties.who_controls: AWS. Customers had no visibility into the control plane dependency until it failed. Post-incident, AWS published guidance on reducing us-east-1 dependencies — effectively admitting the concentration risk they'd built.

properties.title: CrowdStrike July 2024 — largest IT outage in history
properties.affected_scope: 8.5M Windows systems. Airlines (5,078 flights cancelled), banks, hospitals, stock markets, gas stations, emergency services.
properties.one_line: A single faulty sensor update from one security vendor crashed 8.5 million Windows machines worldwide — flights cancelled, hospitals disrupted, emergency services degraded. The largest IT outage in history.
properties.dependency: CrowdStrike Falcon runs at kernel level on Windows systems. Channel file 291 update caused boot loop. Every organization running CrowdStrike on Windows was affected simultaneously. No customer action triggered it.
properties.consequence: 5,078 flights cancelled (4.6% of scheduled). Hospitals reverted to paper records. Emergency dispatch systems degraded. Stock trading disrupted. Tens of billions in estimated damages. Required manual remediation — no remote fix possible for boot-looped machines.
properties.who_controls: CrowdStrike pushed the update. Microsoft's OS architecture allowed kernel-level access. Neither customers nor affected end-users had any lever. The blast radius was set by vendor market share, not by any customer's choice.

properties.title: Fastly CDN outage — 49 minutes, half the internet dark
properties.affected_scope: Reddit, New York Times, The Guardian, Twitch, UK government website, Amazon, eBay, Stack Overflow, Shopify merchants
properties.one_line: A valid customer config change triggered a latent bug in Fastly's CDN. For 49 minutes, Reddit, NYT, UK government, Twitch, and Amazon were unreachable. One CDN vendor = one point of failure for half the visible internet.
properties.dependency: Fastly CDN serves as the edge layer between users and origin servers. Bug deployed May 12 lay dormant until triggered June 8 by a valid config change. 85% of Fastly's network returned errors simultaneously.
properties.consequence: Major news, government, e-commerce, and social platforms unreachable for ~49 minutes. NYT redirected to Google Cloud origin as workaround. UK government services offline. Demonstrated that CDN concentration creates systemic fragility across unrelated organizations.
properties.who_controls: Fastly. The triggering customer didn't do anything wrong. The bug was in Fastly's own deployment from a month earlier. Every Fastly customer inherited the risk.

properties.title: AWS October 2025 — 15-hour DNS failure, 4 million users offline
properties.affected_scope: 4M users, 1,000+ companies, 141 AWS services. Ring doorbells (10M devices offline), smart locks, thermostats.
properties.one_line: Empty DNS record + DynamoDB race condition = 15 hours of outage, 141 AWS services affected, 10 million Ring doorbells offline. Your doorbell is downstream of a database in Virginia.
properties.dependency: DNS resolution failure in us-east-1 caused by empty DNS record. Race condition in DynamoDB prevented recovery. 141 of AWS's own services affected. Ring, smart locks, thermostats, and IoT devices with no offline fallback went dark.
properties.consequence: 10 million Ring devices offline — no video recording, no motion alerts, no remote access. Smart locks unresponsive. 4M end users affected across 1,000+ companies. Demonstrated IoT's total cloud dependency: devices become inert hardware when the connection drops.
properties.who_controls: AWS. Ring is an Amazon subsidiary — even Amazon's own hardware products couldn't survive Amazon's own infrastructure failure. Consumers who bought 'security' devices found their security was downstream of a DNS table.

properties.title: EU data sovereignty — residency without control
properties.affected_scope: EU governments, enterprises, and citizens using US cloud providers
properties.one_line: Microsoft completed its EU Data Boundary in February 2025. The data stays in Europe. The CLOUD Act still applies. Residency is not sovereignty.
properties.dependency: 120+ countries now have data protection laws. EU GDPR requires data residency. But the US CLOUD Act (2018) compels US-based providers to produce data regardless of storage location. Microsoft's EU Data Boundary addresses residency but explicitly does not override CLOUD Act obligations.
properties.consequence: Gaia-X — the EU's sovereign cloud initiative — was captured by US hyperscalers who lobbied for inclusion and diluted sovereignty requirements. EU organizations using AWS/Azure/GCP have data residency but not data sovereignty. 62% of global cloud market controlled by three US companies.
properties.who_controls: US government (via CLOUD Act) and US hyperscalers (via market dominance). EU Data Boundary is a geographic feature, not a legal one. Executive agreements with UK (2019) and Australia (2021) formalize the access mechanism.

properties.title: Loudoun County — where cloud concentration meets grid dependency
properties.provider: AWS, Microsoft, Google, Meta, and others
properties.affected_scope: Global cloud users (via control planes) + 67M PJM ratepayers (via capacity costs)
properties.one_line: World's largest data center concentration. AWS us-east-1 control plane, 115 data centers, $576M in local tax revenue, 833% PJM capacity price spike. Cloud dependency and grid dependency are the same place.
properties.dependency: 115 data centers in one county. AWS alone has 65 (500+ acres). Data centers drove 63% of PJM's $9.3B capacity cost increase and 94% of projected 32GW demand growth. The same physical concentration that makes us-east-1 a cloud chokepoint also makes it a grid chokepoint.
properties.consequence: Cloud users worldwide depend on infrastructure in one county. PJM ratepayers across 13 states subsidize the power for it. $576M annual tax revenue means the county government is fiscally dependent on data center growth. The dependency runs in every direction.
properties.who_controls: Hyperscalers (investment decisions), PJM (market rules), Loudoun County (permitting), Virginia (state policy). No single entity governs the compound exposure. The atlas's US infrastructure cases and cloud cases converge here.

properties.title: Epic on Azure/AWS — 30 health systems, two vendors, no exit plan
properties.affected_scope: 30 North American health systems, millions of patient records
properties.one_line: 30 major health systems now run Epic on AWS or Azure. Epic stopped Google Cloud integrations. Your medical records are downstream of two cloud vendors and one EHR monopoly.
properties.dependency: Epic Systems dominates US hospital EHR market. 30 health systems now run Epic on public cloud (90% AWS, some Azure). Epic stopped Google Cloud integrations, narrowing the vendor pool to two. Healthcare cloud market: $79.5B (2024) → $309.5B (2033).
properties.consequence: Patient records, clinical workflows, medication ordering, and billing all run through one EHR vendor on one or two cloud providers. A cloud outage becomes a clinical safety event. Migration costs and vendor lock-in make exit prohibitively expensive.
properties.who_controls: Epic Systems (EHR), AWS/Azure (infrastructure). Health systems choose Epic but inherit cloud vendor dependency. Patients have no say in any of it. Regulatory oversight (HIPAA) covers data handling, not infrastructure concentration.

properties.title: DNS concentration — half the internet's domains depend on 10 providers
properties.provider: Cloudflare, AWS Route 53, Akamai, and others
properties.affected_scope: 49% of all domain names. 90% of DNS forwarding through 5% of resolvers.
properties.one_line: 49% of all domain names rely on 10 nameserver providers. 98% use a single NS provider. When Facebook's BGP misconfiguration took out its DNS in October 2021, 3.5 billion users lost access for 6 hours.
properties.dependency: DNS is the phone book of the internet. 49% of all domains depend on Top 10 NS providers. 98% of domains use a single NS provider — no redundancy. 5% of indirect resolvers support 90% of all forwarding. BGP routing errors cascade through DNS: one misconfiguration can make entire networks unreachable.
properties.consequence: Facebook October 2021: BGP routing error → authoritative DNS failure → 3.5 billion users offline for 6 hours. Internal tools also went down, preventing engineers from fixing it remotely. Demonstrated that DNS concentration creates systemic risk invisible to users.
properties.who_controls: A handful of DNS/CDN providers. No single authority verifies BGP route announcements. Domain owners choose one NS provider and inherit its failure modes. End users have no visibility into which DNS provider serves the sites they use.

properties.title: Cloud egress pricing — the toll booth you can't avoid
properties.affected_scope: All organizations using hyperscaler cloud services
properties.one_line: Moving 50TB out of AWS costs $3,500-7,000 in egress fees. Cross-AZ pricing discourages resilient architectures. The billing model is a governance layer that shapes what you can build and whether you can leave.
properties.dependency: $0.08-0.12/GB to move data out. 6-12% of typical cloud bills (20-40% for data-heavy orgs). Cross-region pricing incentivizes co-location in one region (reducing resilience). Reserved instances lock organizations into multi-year commitments. 2025: providers reduced egress fees under regulatory pressure, but cross-AZ/NAT gateway costs unchanged.
properties.consequence: Organizations cannot afford to leave — migration cost exceeds switching benefit. Architecture decisions driven by billing rather than resilience. Cross-AZ pricing discourages the very redundancy that would protect against outages. The pricing model enforces concentration.
properties.who_controls: AWS, Azure, GCP set the prices. 62% of global cloud market controlled by three companies. Cloud market at $419B/year (2025), growing 25% YoY. Organizations report vendor lock-in as top concern but cannot afford to act on it.
